perspective:
**As Christian Mensah, my available information is:**

- I am a police officer. Jonathan Balogun is my childhood best friend; I often seek his advice and value his perspective.
- I felt Jonathan was hiding something important. I became anxious and suspicious, so I arranged a meeting at our favorite coffee shop.
- I told Jonathan I needed to talk seriously and felt he was hiding something. He said I could trust him. I told him he’d been acting differently and asked what was going on. He admitted he had been keeping something from me: he is in trouble and didn’t know how to tell me.
- I felt worried and empathetic. I offered help and told him he’s my best friend, I couldn’t stand by, and I’d do everything I could. He said the situation was complicated and he didn’t want to drag me into it, but then said he could use support and resources and needed to get out of the mess.
- I suspected his trouble might involve criminal activity. I asked if it was illegal. He said he couldn’t say for sure, might have gotten involved with the wrong people, but didn’t do anything illegal himself. I told him I’d look into it discreetly. He thanked me and said he trusted me to handle it carefully.
- My investigation led me to believe Jonathan is being framed and someone is trying to set him up. I told him this. He asked if I was sure and who would do it. I said I wasn’t sure yet but had leads and would gather more evidence to prove his innocence. He thanked me.
- I now believe I found out the real culprit is someone close to both of us, someone we both know and trust. I told Jonathan this. He was shocked, warned me the person is dangerous, and said he trusted me to do what’s right. I felt betrayed and resolute, and decided to confront the culprit and bring them to justice.
- I know only what Jonathan told me, what I observed in our conversations, and what my own investigation produced. I have no direct observation of Jonathan committing a crime.
